questions.title: How does the Cayley transform ensure orthogonality of the parameter matrix in OFT and BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that OFT and the butterfly components in BOFT use the Cayley transform, i.e., \(R = (I+Q)(I-Q)^{-1}\) with a skew‑symmetric \(Q\), to keep \(R\) orthogonal during training. I am unclear on two points: (1) why does this parametrization guarantee that \(R\) stays orthogonal for any skew‑symmetric \(Q\)? (2) In practice, how is the inverse \((I-Q)^{-1}\) computed efficiently for large matrices, especially when \(Q\) is block‑diagonal or composed of many small butterfly blocks?

questions.title: What is the exact parameter count for BOFT($m,b$) and how does it compare to block‑diagonal OFT?
questions.question_body: In Section 4 the authors state that BOFT($m,b$) uses \(\frac{1}{2}(b-1)dm\) effective trainable parameters for a layer of size \(d\times n\). I would like a step‑by‑step derivation of this formula. Also, how does this count compare numerically to a block‑diagonal OFT with block size \(b\) (i.e., \(r = d/b\) blocks)? A concrete example with \(d=1024\), \(b=8\), and \(m = \log_2 d = 10\) would be helpful.

questions.title: Why does the butterfly factorization achieve dense connectivity with only \(O(d\log d)\) edges?
questions.question_body: The paper argues that the butterfly graph can connect every source node to every sink node using only \(O(d\log d)\) non‑zero entries, unlike a single dense matrix which needs \(O(d^2)\). Could someone explain intuitively how the recursive butterfly construction guarantees that each input can reach every output? A small illustration for \(d=8\) showing the edge pattern across the log‑depth stages would clarify this.

questions.title: How is multiplicative dropout implemented for the product of butterfly components?
questions.question_body: BOFT introduces a "multiplicative Dropout" where a percentage of butterfly components and a percentage of diagonal blocks within each component are replaced by identity matrices. I am confused about (a) whether the dropout mask is sampled per training step or per layer, (b) how gradients flow through the remaining (non‑dropped) components, and (c) if there is any need to renormalize the orthogonal matrix after dropout.

questions.title: What is the relationship between BOFT’s weight interpolation (Figure 2) and linear interpolation in the orthogonal group?
questions.question_body: The authors claim that BOFT enables an "intriguing weight interpolation" because the orthogonal matrix is a product of several sparse orthogonal factors. Does this mean that interpolating between two sets of BOFT parameters corresponds to moving along a geodesic on the Stiefel manifold, or is it simply a linear interpolation of each factor? How does this affect training stability compared to directly interpolating a full orthogonal matrix?

questions.title: Can BOFT approximate any orthogonal matrix arbitrarily well, and what are the theoretical limits?
questions.question_body:
Theorem 1 states that BOFT is more expressive than block‑diagonal OFT and that multiplying certain butterfly matrices can approximate any orthogonal matrix. However, the theorem’s statement involves products like \(B_{d-1,1}(d) B_{d-1,2}^T(d) \dots B_{1,1}(d) B_{1,2}^T(d)\). I would like clarification on:
1. How many distinct butterfly matrices are required as a function of dimension \(d\)?
2. Does this construction yield an exact representation of any orthogonal matrix or only an approximation?
3. Are there known lower bounds on the number of layers \(m\) or block size \(b\) needed to achieve a given approximation error?

questions.title: Why does preserving pair‑wise neuron angles lead to better generalization in OFT/BOFT?
questions.question_body: The paper motivates orthogonal finetuning by saying that applying an orthogonal transformation preserves pairwise angles between neuron weight vectors, thus retaining pretrained knowledge. Can someone explain more concretely how angle preservation translates into retaining semantic information? Is there empirical evidence linking angle drift to performance degradation in finetuning?

questions.title: How does BOFT’s spectral norm preservation compare to LoRA’s effect on singular values?
questions.question_body: It is claimed that both OFT and BOFT preserve the spectral norm of the pretrained weight matrix because they left‑multiply by an orthogonal matrix, while LoRA adds a low‑rank update which may change singular values. Could anyone provide a simple derivation or experiment showing how LoRA perturbs the singular value spectrum versus BOFT’s exact preservation? Also, does BOFT affect other singular values besides the largest one?

questions.title: What are the practical runtime overheads of BOFT compared to standard OFT?
questions.question_body: The authors note that training with BOFT incurs slightly higher runtime because multiple sparse orthogonal matrices must be multiplied each forward pass. I would like quantitative details: (1) What is the per‑layer additional FLOP count for typical settings (e.g., \(m=\log_2 d, b=2\))? (2) How does this overhead scale with model size (vision transformer vs large language model)? (3) Are there implementation tricks (e.g., fused kernels) that can mitigate this cost?

questions.title: Could alternative network topologies outperform butterfly graphs for dense orthogonal factorization?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions that it is unknown whether butterfly networks are optimal for information transmission under orthogonality constraints. From a graph‑theoretic perspective, what properties should an alternative topology have to reduce edge count while still enabling dense connectivity and respecting orthogonality? Are there known constructions (e.g., Benes networks, expander graphs) that could serve as better factorizations for BOFT?
